questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A voltmeter of resistance $1000 \Omega .0 .5 \mathrm{~V} /$ div is to be converted into a voltmeter to make it to read $=1 \mathrm{~V} / \mathrm{div}$. The value of high resistance to be connected in series with it is
questions.solution:
The sensitivity of the voltmeter is given as $S_1 = 0.5 \text{ V/div}$. The resistance of the voltmeter is $R_V = 1000 \Omega$.

The full scale deflection current $I_g$ is given by $I_g = \dfrac{V_{div}}{R_V} = \dfrac{0.5}{1000} = 5 \times 10^{-4} \text{ A}$.

The new sensitivity required is $S_2 = 1 \text{ V/div}$. Let the new total resistance be $R_{total} = R_V + R_s$, where $R_s$ is the series resistance to be added.

For the new sensitivity, $I_g = \dfrac{S_2}{R_V + R_s}$.

Substituting the values: $5 \times 10^{-4} = \dfrac{1}{1000 + R_s}$.

$1000 + R_s = \dfrac{1}{5 \times 10^{-4}} = \dfrac{10000}{5} = 2000$.

$R_s = 2000 - 1000 = 1000 \Omega$.

Answer: $1000 \Omega$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle of mass $2 \mathrm{mg}$ has the same wavelength as a neutron moving with a velocity of $3 \times 10^5 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$. The velocity of the particle is (mass of neutron is $1.67 \times 10^{-27} \mathrm{Kg}$)
questions.solution:
The de Broglie wavelength $\lambda$ is given by the relation $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{mv}$.

Since the particle and the neutron have the same wavelength, we have $\lambda_{p} = \lambda_{n}$, which implies $m_{p} v_{p} = m_{n} v_{n}$.

Given values are:
Mass of particle $m_{p} = 2 \text{ mg} = 2 \times 10^{-6} \text{ kg}$.
Mass of neutron $m_{n} = 1.67 \times 10^{-27} \text{ kg}$.
Velocity of neutron $v_{n} = 3 \times 10^5 \text{ ms}^{-1}$.

Substituting these values into the equation $v_{p} = \dfrac{m_{n} v_{n}}{m_{p}}$:

$v_{p} = \dfrac{(1.67 \times 10^{-27} \text{ kg}) \times (3 \times 10^5 \text{ ms}^{-1})}{2 \times 10^{-6} \text{ kg}}$

$v_{p} = \dfrac{5.01 \times 10^{-22}}{2 \times 10^{-6}} \text{ ms}^{-1}$

$v_{p} = 2.505 \times 10^{-16} \text{ ms}^{-1}$

Rounding to the nearest provided option, we get $v_{p} = 2.5 \times 10^{-16} \text{ ms}^{-1}$.

Answer: $2.5 \times 10^{-16} \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A photon emitted during the de-excitation of electron from a state $\mathrm{n}$ to the second excited state in a hydrogen atom, irradiates a metallic electrode of work function $0.5 \mathrm{~eV}$, in a photocell, with a stopping voltage of $0.47 \mathrm{~V}$. Obtain the value of quantum number of the state '$n$'.
questions.solution:
The energy of a photon emitted during the transition from state $n$ to the second excited state ($n_f = 3$) in a hydrogen atom is given by the Rydberg formula:

$E = 13.6 \left( \dfrac{1}{n_f^2} - \dfrac{1}{n_i^2} \right) \text{ eV}$

$E = 13.6 \left( \dfrac{1}{3^2} - \dfrac{1}{n^2} \right) = 13.6 \left( \dfrac{1}{9} - \dfrac{1}{n^2} \right) \text{ eV}$

According to Einstein's photoelectric equation, the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons is $K_{max} = E - \Phi$, where $\Phi$ is the work function. Given $K_{max} = e V_s = 0.47 \text{ eV}$ and $\Phi = 0.5 \text{ eV}$:

$0.47 = E - 0.5$

$E = 0.47 + 0.5 = 0.97 \text{ eV}$

Equating the two expressions for $E$:

$13.6 \left( \dfrac{1}{9} - \dfrac{1}{n^2} \right) = 0.97$

$\dfrac{1}{9} - \dfrac{1}{n^2} = \dfrac{0.97}{13.6} \approx 0.07132$

$\dfrac{1}{n^2} = \dfrac{1}{9} - 0.07132 \approx 0.11111 - 0.07132 = 0.03979$

$n^2 = \dfrac{1}{0.03979} \approx 25.13$

$n \approx 5$

Answer: 5

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The current in a coil changes steadily from $3 \mathrm{~A}$ to $5 \mathrm{~A}$ in $0.2 \mathrm{~s}$ when an emf of $2 \mu \mathrm{V}$ is induced in it. The self-inductance of the coil is
questions.solution:
The induced emf $\varepsilon$ in a coil due to a change in current is given by the formula $\varepsilon = L \left| \dfrac{di}{dt} \right|$, where $L$ is the self-inductance of the coil.

Given values are:
Change in current $\Delta i = 5 \text{ A} - 3 \text{ A} = 2 \text{ A}$
Time interval $\Delta t = 0.2 \text{ s}$
Induced emf $\varepsilon = 2 \mu \text{V} = 2 \times 10^{-6} \text{ V}$

The rate of change of current is $\dfrac{di}{dt} = \dfrac{\Delta i}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{2 \text{ A}}{0.2 \text{ s}} = 10 \text{ A/s}$.

Substituting these values into the formula:
$2 \times 10^{-6} \text{ V} = L \times 10 \text{ A/s}$

$L = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-6}}{10} \text{ H}$

$L = 0.2 \times 10^{-6} \text{ H} = 0.2 \mu \text{H}$.

Answer: 0.2 $\mu H$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A conducting circular loop is placed in a uniform magnetic field $\mathrm{B}=0.125 \mathrm{~T}$ with its plane perpendicular to the loop. If the radius of the loop is made to shrink at a constant rate of $2 \mathrm{~mm} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$, then the induced emf when the radius is $4 \mathrm{~cm}$ is
questions.solution:
The magnetic flux $\Phi$ through the circular loop is given by $\Phi = B A = B (\pi r^2)$, where $B$ is the magnetic field and $r$ is the radius of the loop.

The induced electromotive force (emf) $\varepsilon$ is given by Faraday's law of induction: $\varepsilon = -\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt}$.

Since $B$ is constant, $\varepsilon = -\dfrac{d}{dt}(B \pi r^2) = -B \pi (2r \dfrac{dr}{dt}) = -2 \pi B r \dfrac{dr}{dt}$.

Given $B = 0.125 \text{ T}$, $r = 4 \text{ cm} = 0.04 \text{ m}$, and the rate of shrinking $\dfrac{dr}{dt} = -2 \text{ mm s}^{-1} = -2 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Substituting these values into the expression for magnitude of induced emf:

$|\varepsilon| = 2 \pi (0.125) (0.04) (2 \times 10^{-3})$

$|\varepsilon| = 2 \pi (\dfrac{1}{8}) (4 \times 10^{-2}) (2 \times 10^{-3})$

$|\varepsilon| = 2 \pi (\dfrac{1}{8}) (8 \times 10^{-5}) = 2 \pi \times 10^{-5} \text{ V}$.

Converting to microvolts ($\mu V$):

$|\varepsilon| = 2 \pi \times 10^{-5} \times 10^{6} \mu V = 20 \pi \mu V$.

Answer: $20 \pi \mu V$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The magnetic flux linked with a coil is given by the equation: $\phi = 8t^2 + t + 10$. The e.m.f. induced in the coil at $t = 3$ seconds will be:
questions.solution:
The magnetic flux linked with the coil is given by $\phi = 8t^2 + t + 10$.

The induced electromotive force (e.m.f.) in the coil is given by Faraday's law of induction: $\varepsilon = -\dfrac{d\phi}{dt}$.

Differentiating the flux with respect to time $t$:
$\dfrac{d\phi}{dt} = \dfrac{d}{dt}(8t^2 + t + 10) = 16t + 1$.

The magnitude of the induced e.m.f. is $|\varepsilon| = |-(16t + 1)| = 16t + 1$.

The e.m.f. induced in the $3^{\text{rd}}$ second refers to the instantaneous e.m.f. at $t = 3$ s.

Substituting $t = 3$ into the expression for the magnitude of the e.m.f.:
$|\varepsilon| = 16(3) + 1 = 48 + 1 = 49$ V.

Answer: 49 V

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Column - I lists the waves of the electromagnetic spectrum. Column - II gives approximate frequency range of these waves. Match Column - I and Column - II and choose the correct match from the given choices.
No.Column INo.Column II
ARadiowavesP$10^{18}$ to $10^{20}$ Hz
BMicrowavesQ$10^{11}$ to $5 \times 10^{14}$ Hz
CInfraredR$10^{4}$ to $10^{8}$ Hz
DX-raysS$10^{9}$ to $10^{12}$ Hz
questions.solution:
The electromagnetic spectrum is categorized by frequency ranges as follows:

Radiowaves have a frequency range typically from $10^4 \text{ Hz}$ to $10^8 \text{ Hz}$. This matches (A) with (R).

Microwaves have a frequency range typically from $10^9 \text{ Hz}$ to $10^{12} \text{ Hz}$. This matches (B) with (S).

Infrared radiation has a frequency range from approximately $10^{11} \text{ Hz}$ to $5 \times 10^{14} \text{ Hz}$. This matches (C) with (Q).

X-rays have a frequency range typically from $10^{18} \text{ Hz}$ to $10^{20} \text{ Hz}$. This matches (D) with (P).

Therefore, the correct matching is (A)-(R), (B)-(S), (C)-(Q), and (D)-(P).

Answer: (A)-(R) (B)-(S) (C)-(Q) (D)-(P)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A neutral water molecule, modeled as an electric dipole with an effective charge equal to one elementary charge ($e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$), is placed in an electric field $E = 2.5 \times 10^4 \text{ NC}^{-1}$. The work done to rotate it by $180^\circ$ from its stable equilibrium position is $5 \times 10^{-25} \text{ J}$. Find the approximate separation of the centre of charges.
questions.solution:
Work done to rotate dipole by $180°$ from stable equilibrium:

$W = pE(\cos 0° - \cos 180°) = 2pE$

$p = \dfrac{W}{2E} = \dfrac{5 \times 10^{-25}}{2 \times 2.5 \times 10^4} = \dfrac{5 \times 10^{-25}}{5 \times 10^4} = 10^{-29}$ C m

$p = qd \Rightarrow d = \dfrac{p}{q} = \dfrac{10^{-29}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} = 0.625 \times 10^{-10}$ m

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If 216 drops of the same size are charged at $200 \mathrm{~V}$ each and they combine to form a bigger drop, the potential of the bigger drop will be
questions.solution:
Let $r$ be the radius of each small drop and $q$ be the charge on each small drop. The potential of a small drop is given by $V = \dfrac{kq}{r} = 200 \text{ V}$.

When $n = 216$ drops combine to form a bigger drop of radius $R$ and charge $Q$, the volume remains conserved. Thus, $\dfrac{4}{3} \pi R^3 = n \times \dfrac{4}{3} \pi r^3$, which implies $R = n^{1/3} r$.

Substituting $n = 216$, we get $R = (216)^{1/3} r = 6r$.

The total charge on the bigger drop is $Q = nq = 216q$.

The potential of the bigger drop $V'$ is given by $V' = \dfrac{kQ}{R} = \dfrac{k(nq)}{n^{1/3}r} = n^{2/3} \times \dfrac{kq}{r}$.

Substituting the values, $V' = (216)^{2/3} \times 200 = (6^3)^{2/3} \times 200 = 6^2 \times 200 = 36 \times 200 = 7200 \text{ V}$.

Answer: 7200 V

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two point charges $\mathrm{M}$ and $\mathrm{N}$ having charges $+q$ and $-q$ respectively are placed at a distance apart. Force acting between them is $\mathrm{F}$. If $30 \%$ of charge of $\mathrm{N}$ is transferred to $\mathrm{M}$, then the force between the charges becomes:
questions.solution:
Initial force: $F = \dfrac{kq^2}{r^2}$

30% of charge of N transferred to M:
Charge transferred $= 0.3q$
New charge on M $= +q + (-0.3q) = 0.7q$
New charge on N $= -q - (-0.3q) = -0.7q$

$F' = \dfrac{k(0.7q)(0.7q)}{r^2} = 0.49 \cdot \dfrac{kq^2}{r^2} = \dfrac{49}{100}F$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Three point charges are located on a circular arc at A, B and C as shown in the figure below. The total electric field at the centre of the arc (0) is
questions.solution:
$r = 6.0$ cm $= 0.06$ m, $r^2 = 0.0036$ m$^2$

$E_A = E_B = \dfrac{(9 \times 10^9)(4.0 \times 10^{-9})}{0.0036} = 10000$ N/C (away from A and B)

$E_C = \dfrac{(9 \times 10^9)(2.0 \times 10^{-9})}{0.0036} = 5000$ N/C (towards C, since charge is negative)

By symmetry, A and B are $60°$ on either side of OC axis. Their perpendicular components cancel. Only components along OC axis are considered:

$E_{net} = E_C - E_A\cos60° - E_B\cos60°$
$= 5000 - 10000(0.5) - 10000(0.5)$
$= 5000 - 5000 - 5000 = -5000$ N/C

Magnitude $= 5000$ NC$^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A satellite is revolving around the earth in a circular orbit with kinetic energy of $1.69 \times 10^{10} \mathrm{~J}$. The additional kinetic energy required for just escaping into the outer space is
questions.solution:
For a satellite in a circular orbit of radius $r$ around the earth of mass $M$, the gravitational potential energy is $U = -\dfrac{GMm}{r}$ and the kinetic energy is $K = \dfrac{GMm}{2r}$.

The total mechanical energy of the satellite in the orbit is $E = K + U = \dfrac{GMm}{2r} - \dfrac{GMm}{r} = -\dfrac{GMm}{2r} = -K$.

Given $K = 1.69 \times 10^{10} \text{ J}$, the total energy is $E = -1.69 \times 10^{10} \text{ J}$.

To escape into outer space, the final total energy of the satellite must be at least $0$.

The required additional energy $\Delta E$ is given by $E_{final} - E_{initial} = 0 - E = -(-K) = K$.

Therefore, the additional kinetic energy required is equal to the current kinetic energy, which is $1.69 \times 10^{10} \text{ J}$.

Answer: $1.69 \times 10^{10} \mathrm{~J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The acceleration due to gravity at pole and equator can be related as
questions.solution:
The acceleration due to gravity $g$ at a point on the surface of the Earth at a latitude $\lambda$ is given by the formula $g_{\lambda} = g - R\omega^2 \cos^2 \lambda$, where $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity at the poles, $R$ is the radius of the Earth, and $\omega$ is the angular velocity of the Earth.

At the poles, the latitude $\lambda = 90^{\circ}$. Substituting this into the formula, we get $g_p = g - R\omega^2 \cos^2(90^{\circ}) = g - 0 = g$.

At the equator, the latitude $\lambda = 0^{\circ}$. Substituting this into the formula, we get $g_e = g - R\omega^2 \cos^2(0^{\circ}) = g - R\omega^2$.

Since $R\omega^2 \gt 0$, it follows that $g - R\omega^2 \lt g$. Therefore, $g_e \lt g_p$.

Answer: $g_e \lt g_p$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Internal energy of $\mathrm{n}_1$ moles of hydrogen at temperature T is equal to internal energy of $\mathrm{m}_2$ moles of helium at temperature 2T. The ratio $\dfrac{n_1}{n_2}$ is
questions.solution:
The internal energy $U$ of an ideal gas is given by $U = n C_V T$, where $n$ is the number of moles, $C_V$ is the molar heat capacity at constant volume, and $T$ is the temperature.

For hydrogen ($H_2$), which is a diatomic gas, the degrees of freedom $f = 5$. Thus, $C_{V, H_2} = \dfrac{f}{2} R = \dfrac{5}{2} R$. The internal energy is $U_1 = n_1 \times \dfrac{5}{2} R \times T$.

For helium ($He$), which is a monatomic gas, the degrees of freedom $f = 3$. Thus, $C_{V, He} = \dfrac{f}{2} R = \dfrac{3}{2} R$. The internal energy is $U_2 = n_2 \times \dfrac{3}{2} R \times (2T)$.

Equating the internal energies $U_1 = U_2$:

$n_1 \times \dfrac{5}{2} R \times T = n_2 \times \dfrac{3}{2} R \times 2T$

Simplifying the equation by cancelling $R$ and $T$ from both sides:

$n_1 \times \dfrac{5}{2} = n_2 \times 3$

Rearranging to find the ratio $\dfrac{n_1}{n_2}$:

$\dfrac{n_1}{n_2} = \dfrac{3}{5/2} = \dfrac{3 \times 2}{5} = \dfrac{6}{5}$

Answer: $\dfrac{6}{5}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body initially at rest undergoes rectilinear motion. The forcetime (F-t) graph for the motion of the body is given below. Find the linear momentum gained by the body in $2 \mathrm{~s}$.
questions.solution:
The impulse $J$ delivered to a body is equal to the change in its linear momentum $\Delta p$.

The impulse is given by the area under the force-time ($F-t$) graph.

For the interval $t = 0$ to $t = 2$ s, the graph represents a semi-circle below the time axis with radius $r = 1$ s and amplitude $A = 4$ N.

The area of this semi-circle is $A_{area} = \dfrac{1}{2} \pi r^2$.

Since the area is below the time axis, the impulse is negative: $J = -\dfrac{1}{2} \pi (1)^2 = -\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ N-s.

The magnitude of the linear momentum gained is $|J| = \left| -\dfrac{\pi}{2} \right| = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ N-s.

Answer: $\dfrac{\pi}{2} \mathrm{~N}-\mathrm{s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Action and reaction can never balance out because
options: They are equal in magnitude but not opposite always.
They are unequal in magnitudes even though opposite in direction
Though they are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction they act on different bodies.
questions.solution:
According to Newton's third law of motion, for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.

These two forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.

However, the fundamental reason they do not balance each other out is that they act on two different bodies. Since the forces are applied to different objects, they cannot result in the net force on a single body being zero.

Answer: Though they are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction they act on different bodies.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A negative charge particle is moving upward in a magnetic field which is towards north. The particle is deflected towards
questions.solution:
The force on a moving charge in a magnetic field is given by the Lorentz force formula $\vec{F} = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$.

Here, the charge $q$ is negative. The velocity vector $\vec{v}$ is directed upward (along the positive z-axis, $\hat{k}$), and the magnetic field $\vec{B}$ is directed towards the north (along the positive y-axis, $\hat{j}$).

The cross product $\vec{v} \times \vec{B}$ is $\hat{k} \times \hat{j} = -\hat{i}$, which points towards the west.

Since the charge $q$ is negative, the force $\vec{F} = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})$ will be in the direction opposite to $\vec{v} \times \vec{B}$.

Therefore, the force is directed towards the east.

Answer: East

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A wire of length $2 \mathrm{~m}$ carries a current of $1 \mathrm{~A}$ along the $\mathrm{x}$ axis. A magnetic field $B=B_0(i+j+k)$ tesla exists in space.
The magnitude of magnetic force on the wire is
questions.solution:
The magnetic force on a current-carrying wire is given by the formula $\vec{F} = I(\vec{L} \times \vec{B})$.

The length vector $\vec{L}$ of the wire is $2\hat{i}$ m, as it lies along the x-axis and has a length of $2$ m. The current $I$ is $1$ A.

The magnetic field is given as $\vec{B} = B_0(\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k})$.

Substituting these values into the force equation:
$\vec{F} = 1 \times (2\hat{i}) \times B_0(\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k})$
$\vec{F} = 2B_0 [(\hat{i} \times \hat{i}) + (\hat{i} \times \hat{j}) + (\hat{i} \times \hat{k})]$

Using the cross product properties $\hat{i} \times \hat{i} = 0$, $\hat{i} \times \hat{j} = \hat{k}$, and $\hat{i} \times \hat{k} = -\hat{j}$:
$\vec{F} = 2B_0 [0 + \hat{k} - \hat{j}] = 2B_0(\hat{k} - \hat{j})$

The magnitude of the force is $|\vec{F}| = |2B_0| \sqrt{(1)^2 + (-1)^2} = 2B_0 \sqrt{2}$.

Answer: 2$\sqrt2$B_0$ N$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A current I flows in an infinitely long wire with cross section in the form of semi-circular ring of radius $1 \mathrm{~m}$. The magnitude of the magnetic induction along its axis is
questions.solution:
Current per unit angle: $dI = \dfrac{I}{\pi}d\theta$

Magnetic field due to element (infinite wire) at axis (distance $R$):

$dB = \dfrac{\mu_0 dI}{2\pi R} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi^2 R}d\theta$

By symmetry, only sine components add up:

$B_{net} = \int_0^{\pi} dB\sin\theta = \int_0^{\pi} \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi^2 R}\sin\theta \, d\theta$

$= \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi^2 R}[-\cos\theta]_0^{\pi}$

$= \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi^2 R}[1+1] = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{\pi^2 R}$

For $R = 1$ m:

$B_{net} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{\pi^2}$ T

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A bar magnet is held perpendicular to a uniform field. If the couple acting on the magnet is to be halved, by rotating it, the angle by which it is to be rotated is
questions.solution:
The torque acting on a bar magnet in a uniform magnetic field is given by $\tau = MB \sin \theta$, where $M$ is the magnetic moment, $B$ is the magnetic field, and $\theta$ is the angle between the magnetic moment vector and the magnetic field vector.

Initially, the magnet is held perpendicular to the field, so $\theta_1 = 90^{\circ}$. The initial torque is $\tau_1 = MB \sin 90^{\circ} = MB$.

The problem states that the torque is to be halved, so the new torque $\tau_2 = \dfrac{MB}{2}$.

Substituting the new torque into the formula: $\dfrac{MB}{2} = MB \sin \theta_2$, which simplifies to $\sin \theta_2 = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

This gives $\theta_2 = 30^{\circ}$.

The angle by which the magnet is rotated is $\Delta \theta = \theta_1 - \theta_2 = 90^{\circ} - 30^{\circ} = 60^{\circ}$.

Answer: $60^{\circ}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: For a paramagnetic material, the dependence of the magnetic susceptibility $\chi$ on the absolute temperature is given as
questions.solution:
According to Curie's Law, the magnetic susceptibility $\chi$ of a paramagnetic material is inversely proportional to its absolute temperature $T$.

The mathematical expression for Curie's Law is given by $\chi = \dfrac{C}{T}$, where $C$ is the Curie constant.

Therefore, $\chi \propto \dfrac{1}{T}$.

Answer: $X \propto\dfrac{1}{T}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: What is the relation obeyed by the angles of contact $\theta_1, \theta_2$ and $\theta_3$ of 3 liquids of different densities $P_1, P_2$ and $P_3$ respectively $(\mathrm{P}_1 \lt  \mathrm{P}_2 \lt  \mathrm{P}_3$) when they rise to the same capillary height in 3 identical capillaries and having nearly same surface tension $\mathrm{T}$ ?
questions.solution:
From Jurin's law: $h = \dfrac{2T\cos\theta}{rPg}$

Since $h$, $T$, $r$, $g$ are constant: $\cos\theta \propto P$

Given $P_1 \lt P_2 \lt P_3$:

$\cos\theta_1 \lt \cos\theta_2 \lt \cos\theta_3$

Since liquids rise ($h \gt 0$), $\cos\theta \gt 0$, so all angles are acute: $0 \leq \theta \lt \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

In $\left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$, cosine is decreasing, so smaller cosine means larger angle:

$\theta_1 \gt \theta_2 \gt \theta_3$

Combined: $\dfrac{\pi}{2} \gt \theta_1 \gt \theta_2 \gt \theta_3 \geq 0$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The temperature of a wire is doubled. The Young's modulus of elasticity
questions.solution:
Young's modulus of elasticity $Y$ is a material property that depends primarily on the nature of the material and the temperature. When the temperature of a solid increases, the interatomic distances increase due to thermal expansion, which weakens the interatomic forces.

As the temperature increases, the atomic vibrations increase, leading to a decrease in the stiffness of the material. Consequently, the Young's modulus of elasticity decreases with an increase in temperature.

Therefore, when the temperature of a wire is doubled, its Young's modulus of elasticity will decrease.

Answer: Will decrease

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A cricketer of height $2.5 \mathrm{~m}$ throws a ball at an angle of $30^{\circ}$ with the horizontal such that it is received by another cricketer of same height standing at a distance of $50 \mathrm{~m}$ from the first one. The maximum height attained by the ball is ($\tan 30^{\circ}=0.577$)
questions.solution:
The height of both cricketers is $h = 2.5 \text{ m}$. Since the ball is thrown and received at the same height, the vertical displacement is zero. The horizontal range $R$ is given by $R = \dfrac{u^2 \sin(2\theta)}{g}$.

Given $R = 50 \text{ m}$ and $\theta = 30^{\circ}$, we have $50 = \dfrac{u^2 \sin(60^{\circ})}{g} = \dfrac{u^2 \sqrt{3}}{2g}$.

Thus, $\dfrac{u^2}{g} = \dfrac{100}{\sqrt{3}}$.

The maximum height $H$ attained by the projectile above the point of projection is given by $H = \dfrac{u^2 \sin^2 \theta}{2g}$.

Substituting the value of $\dfrac{u^2}{g}$:

$H = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \left( \dfrac{u^2}{g} \right) \times \sin^2(30^{\circ}) = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{100}{\sqrt{3}} \times \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right)^2 = \dfrac{100}{8\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{12.5}{1.732} \approx 7.216 \text{ m}$.

The total maximum height from the ground is $H_{total} = h + H = 2.5 + 7.216 = 9.716 \text{ m}$.

Rounding to the nearest value provided in the options, we get $9.7 \text{ m}$.

Answer: 9.7 m

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A ball is moving in a circular path of radius $5 \mathrm{~m}$. If tangential acceleration at any instant is $10 \mathrm{~ms}^{-2}$ and the net acceleration makes an angle of $30^{\circ}$ with the centripetal acceleration, then, the instantaneous speed is
questions.solution:
The tangential acceleration is given as $a_t = 10 \mathrm{~ms}^{-2}$.

The centripetal acceleration is given by $a_c = \dfrac{v^2}{r}$, where $v$ is the instantaneous speed and $r = 5 \mathrm{~m}$. Thus, $a_c = \dfrac{v^2}{5}$.

The net acceleration $\vec{a}$ is the vector sum of the tangential acceleration $\vec{a}_t$ and the centripetal acceleration $\vec{a}_c$. Since $\vec{a}_t$ and $\vec{a}_c$ are perpendicular, the angle $\theta$ between the net acceleration $\vec{a}$ and the centripetal acceleration $\vec{a}_c$ is given by $\tan \theta = \dfrac{a_t}{a_c}$.

Given $\theta = 30^{\circ}$, we have $\tan 30^{\circ} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$.

Substituting the values, $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{10}{v^2 / 5} = \dfrac{50}{v^2}$.

Therefore, $v^2 = 50 \sqrt{3}$.

Calculating the value, $v^2 = 50 \times 1.732 = 86.6$.

$v = \sqrt{86.6} \approx 9.3 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$.

Answer: $9.3 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: $\text { If the nuclear radius of }{ }^{27} \mathrm{Al} \text { is } 3.6 \text { fermi, the nuclear radius of }{ }^{125} \mathrm{Fe} \text { is }$
questions.solution:
The nuclear radius $R$ is given by the formula $R = R_0 A^{1/3}$, where $R_0$ is a constant and $A$ is the mass number of the nucleus.

For $^{27}\mathrm{Al}$, the mass number $A_1 = 27$ and the radius $R_1 = 3.6 \text{ fermi}$.

Using the formula, $3.6 = R_0 (27)^{1/3} = R_0 \times 3$, which gives $R_0 = 1.2 \text{ fermi}$.

For $^{125}\mathrm{Fe}$, the mass number $A_2 = 125$. The radius $R_2$ is given by $R_2 = R_0 (125)^{1/3} = 1.2 \times 5 = 6.0 \text{ fermi}$.

Since $1 \text{ fermi} = 10^{-15} \text{ m}$, the radius $R_2 = 6.0 \times 10^{-15} \text{ m}$.

Answer: $6 \times 10^{-15} \mathrm{~m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The binding energy per nucleon for $\mathrm{C}^{12}$ is $7.68 \mathrm{~MeV}$ and that for $\mathrm{C}^{13}$ is $7.47 \mathrm{~MeV}$. The energy required to remove a neutron from $\mathrm{C}^{13}$ is
questions.solution:
The binding energy of a nucleus is given by $BE = A \times (BE/A)$, where $A$ is the mass number and $BE/A$ is the binding energy per nucleon.

For $\mathrm{C}^{12}$, $BE_{12} = 12 \times 7.68 \text{ MeV} = 92.16 \text{ MeV}$.

For $\mathrm{C}^{13}$, $BE_{13} = 13 \times 7.47 \text{ MeV} = 97.11 \text{ MeV}$.

The energy required to remove a neutron from $\mathrm{C}^{13}$ is the difference in binding energies: $\Delta E = BE_{13} - BE_{12} = 97.11 \text{ MeV} - 92.16 \text{ MeV} = 4.95 \text{ MeV}$.

Converting this energy to Joules using $1 \text{ MeV} = 1.6 \times 10^{-13} \text{ J}$:

$\Delta E = 4.95 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-13} \text{ J} = 7.92 \times 10^{-13} \text{ J}$.

Answer: $7.92 \times 10^{-13} \mathrm{~J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body is executing SHM. When its displacements from the mean position are $4 \mathrm{~cm}$ and $5 \mathrm{~cm}$ it has velocity $10 \mathrm{~cms}^{-1}$ and $8 \mathrm{~cms}^{-1}$ respectively. Its periodic time $\mathrm{t}$ is
questions.solution:
The velocity $v$ of a particle executing simple harmonic motion at a displacement $x$ is given by $v = \omega \sqrt{A^2 - x^2}$, where $A$ is the amplitude and $\omega$ is the angular frequency.

For the first case, $10 = \omega \sqrt{A^2 - 4^2} \Rightarrow 100 = \omega^2 (A^2 - 16)$.

For the second case, $8 = \omega \sqrt{A^2 - 5^2} \Rightarrow 64 = \omega^2 (A^2 - 25)$.

Dividing the two equations: $\dfrac{100}{64} = \dfrac{A^2 - 16}{A^2 - 25} \Rightarrow \dfrac{25}{16} = \dfrac{A^2 - 16}{A^2 - 25}$.

Cross-multiplying: $25(A^2 - 25) = 16(A^2 - 16) \Rightarrow 25A^2 - 625 = 16A^2 - 256$.

$9A^2 = 369 \Rightarrow A^2 = 41$.

Substituting $A^2 = 41$ into the first equation: $100 = \omega^2 (41 - 16) = 25 \omega^2$.

$\omega^2 = 4 \Rightarrow \omega = 2 \text{ rad s}^{-1}$.

The periodic time $T$ is given by $T = \dfrac{2\pi}{\omega} = \dfrac{2\pi}{2} = \pi \text{ sec}$.

Answer: $\pi$ sec

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Figure below shows a lens of refractive index, $\mu=1.4$. $C_1$ and $C_2$ are the centres of curvature of the two faces of the lens of radii of curvature $4 \mathrm{~cm}$ and $8 \mathrm{~cm}$ respectively. The lens behaves as a
questions.solution:
The lens shown is a meniscus lens. We use the lens maker's formula: $\dfrac{1}{f} = (\mu - 1) \left( \dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2} \right)$.

For the given lens, the first surface (left) is convex towards the object space, so its center of curvature $C_1$ is to the right. By sign convention, $R_1 = +4 \text{ cm}$.

The second surface (right) is also convex towards the object space, so its center of curvature $C_2$ is also to the right. By sign convention, $R_2 = +8 \text{ cm}$.

Given $\mu = 1.4$, we substitute these values into the formula:

$\dfrac{1}{f} = (1.4 - 1) \left( \dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{8} \right)$

$\dfrac{1}{f} = 0.4 \times \left( \dfrac{2 - 1}{8} \right)$

$\dfrac{1}{f} = 0.4 \times \dfrac{1}{8} = \dfrac{0.4}{8} = \dfrac{4}{80} = \dfrac{1}{20}$

Therefore, $f = +20 \text{ cm}$. Since the focal length is positive, the lens behaves as a converging lens.

Answer: converging lens of focal length $20 \mathrm{~cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
When a biconvex lens of glass of refractive index 1.5 is dipped in a liquid, it acts like a plane sheet of paper.
This means the refractive index of the liquid is
questions.solution:
The lens maker formula is given by $\dfrac{1}{f} = (\mu_{rel} - 1) \left( \dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2} \right)$, where $\mu_{rel} = \dfrac{\mu_{lens}}{\mu_{liquid}}$.

When the lens acts like a plane sheet of paper, its focal length $f$ becomes infinite, which implies $\dfrac{1}{f} = 0$.

Substituting this into the lens maker formula, we get $(\mu_{rel} - 1) = 0$, which means $\mu_{rel} = 1$.

Since $\mu_{rel} = \dfrac{\mu_{lens}}{\mu_{liquid}}$, we have $\dfrac{\mu_{lens}}{\mu_{liquid}} = 1$, implying $\mu_{liquid} = \mu_{lens}$.

Given the refractive index of the glass lens is 1.5, the refractive index of the liquid must be equal to 1.5, which is equal to that of the glass.

Answer: Equal to that of glass

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A hollow prism is filled with water and placed in air. It will deviate the incident rays
options: Towards or away from the base
questions.solution:
A prism is a transparent medium bounded by two non-parallel refracting surfaces. When a light ray passes through a prism, it undergoes refraction at both surfaces.

According to Snell's law, when light travels from a rarer medium (air) to a denser medium (water), it bends towards the normal. When it travels from a denser medium (water) to a rarer medium (air), it bends away from the normal.

In a prism, the angle of deviation is determined by the geometry of the prism and the refractive index of the material. For any prism where the refractive index of the material is greater than the refractive index of the surrounding medium, the light ray is always deviated towards the base of the prism.

Since the refractive index of water ($n \approx 1.33$) is greater than the refractive index of air ($n \approx 1.0$), the hollow prism filled with water acts as a converging prism. Therefore, the incident rays are deviated towards the base.

Answer: Towards the base

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A telescope has an objective of focal length 60 cm and eyepiece of focal length 5 cm. The telescope is focussed for least distance of distinct vision for an object 300 cm away. The linear magnification produced by the telescope is:
questions.solution:
For objective lens: $f_o = 60$ cm, $u_o = -300$ cm

$\dfrac{1}{v_o} = \dfrac{1}{f_o} + \dfrac{1}{u_o} = \dfrac{1}{60} - \dfrac{1}{300} = \dfrac{4}{300}$

$v_o = 75$ cm

$m_o = \dfrac{v_o}{u_o} = \dfrac{75}{-300} = -\dfrac{1}{4}$

For eyepiece: $f_e = 5$ cm, image at $D = 25$ cm, so $v_e = -25$ cm

$m_e = 1 - \dfrac{v_e}{f_e} = 1 - \dfrac{-25}{5} = 1 + 5 = 6$

Total magnification: $m = m_o \times m_e = -\dfrac{1}{4} \times 6 = -1.5$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A solid cylinder of mass $2 \mathrm{~kg}$ and radius $0.2 \mathrm{~m}$ is rotating about its own axis without friction with angular velocity $5 \mathrm{~rad} \mathrm{s}^{-1}$. A particle of mass $1 \mathrm{~kg}$ moving with a velocity of $5 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$ strikes the cylinder and sticks to it as shown in figure. The angular velocity of the system after the particle sticks to it will be
questions.solution:
The initial angular momentum of the system about the axis of rotation is the sum of the angular momentum of the cylinder and the angular momentum of the particle. The cylinder is rotating about its own axis, so its angular momentum is $L_{cyl} = I \omega = (\dfrac{1}{2} M R^2) \omega$.

Given $M = 2 \text{ kg}$, $R = 0.2 \text{ m}$, and $\omega = 5 \text{ rad s}^{-1}$, we have $I = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 2 \times (0.2)^2 = 0.04 \text{ kg m}^2$. Thus, $L_{cyl} = 0.04 \times 5 = 0.2 \text{ kg m}^2 \text{s}^{-1}$.

The particle of mass $m = 1 \text{ kg}$ moves with velocity $v = 5 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ at a perpendicular distance $R = 0.2 \text{ m}$ from the axis. Its angular momentum is $L_{part} = m v R = 1 \times 5 \times 0.2 = 1.0 \text{ kg m}^2 \text{s}^{-1}$.

The total initial angular momentum is $L_{initial} = L_{cyl} + L_{part} = 0.2 + 1.0 = 1.2 \text{ kg m}^2 \text{s}^{-1}$.

After the particle sticks to the cylinder, the new moment of inertia is $I' = I + m R^2 = 0.04 + 1 \times (0.2)^2 = 0.04 + 0.04 = 0.08 \text{ kg m}^2$.

By conservation of angular momentum, $L_{initial} = L_{final} = I' \omega'$.

$1.2 = 0.08 \times \omega'$.

$\omega' = \dfrac{1.2}{0.08} = \dfrac{120}{8} = 15.0 \text{ rad s}^{-1}$.

Answer: $15.0 \mathrm{~rad~s}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
The conductivity of a semiconductor increases with increase in temperature because
A) number density of free current carriers increases
B) relaxation time increases
C) both number density of carriers and relaxation time increase
D) number density of current carriers increases, relaxation time decreases but effect of decrease in relaxation time is much less than increase in number density
questions.solution:
The conductivity $\sigma$ of a semiconductor is given by the relation $\sigma = e(n_e \mu_e + n_h \mu_h)$, where $n_e$ and $n_h$ are the number densities of electrons and holes, and $\mu_e$ and $\mu_h$ are their respective mobilities.

As temperature increases, the thermal energy provided to the valence electrons allows them to jump across the band gap into the conduction band, leading to an exponential increase in the number density of charge carriers ($n_e$ and $n_h$).

The mobility $\mu$ is related to the relaxation time $\tau$ by $\mu = \dfrac{e\tau}{m}$. With an increase in temperature, the lattice vibrations increase, which leads to more frequent collisions of charge carriers, thereby decreasing the relaxation time $\tau$.

However, in semiconductors, the increase in the number density of charge carriers is exponential and dominates the effect of the decrease in relaxation time. Consequently, the overall conductivity increases with temperature.

Answer: D

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The output of the given circuit is A. Negatively rectified half wave B. Positively rectified half wave C. Negatively rectified full wave D. Zero all times
questions.solution:
The circuit is a shunt clipper with the diode's anode connected to the top wire and cathode to the bottom (common) wire — diode points downward.

During positive half-cycle ($V_{in} \gt 0$): diode is forward-biased \Rightarrow acts as short circuit $\RightarrowV_{out} = 0$

During negative half-cycle ($V_{in} \lt 0$): diode is reverse-biased \Rightarrow acts as open circuit \Rightarrow no drop across R $\RightarrowV_{out} = V_{in}$

Only the negative half-cycle appears at the output \Rightarrow negatively rectified half wave (option A).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
The following are the graphs of potential barrier versus width of the depletion region for a p-n junction diode. Which of the following is correct?
IIIIIIIV
A - unbiased diodeA - Forward biased diodeA - unbiased diodeA - unbiased diode
B - Reverse biasedB - Reverse biasedB - Forward biasedB - unused diode
C - Forward biasedC - unbiasedC - Reverse biasedC - Forward biased
questions.solution:
Forward biased diode: external voltage opposes built-in potential \Rightarrow reduced barrier height and narrower depletion region \Rightarrow Graph C (lowest, narrowest).

Reverse biased diode: external voltage adds to built-in potential \Rightarrow increased barrier and wider depletion region \Rightarrow Graph B (highest, widest).

Unbiased diode: natural built-in potential, intermediate width \Rightarrow Graph A.

Matching: A - unbiased, B - reverse biased, C - forward biased \Rightarrow Column I is correct.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The coefficient of volume expansion of glycerine is $49 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}$. The percentage change in its density for a $50^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ rise in temperature is
questions.solution:
The density $\rho$ of a liquid at temperature $T$ is related to its density $\rho_0$ at initial temperature $T_0$ by the relation $\rho = \dfrac{\rho_0}{1 + \gamma \Delta T}$, where $\gamma$ is the coefficient of volume expansion and $\Delta T$ is the change in temperature.

The change in density $\Delta \rho = \rho - \rho_0 = \rho_0 \left( \dfrac{1}{1 + \gamma \Delta T} - 1 \right) = \rho_0 \left( \dfrac{1 - 1 - \gamma \Delta T}{1 + \gamma \Delta T} \right) = - \dfrac{\rho_0 \gamma \Delta T}{1 + \gamma \Delta T}$.

For small values of $\gamma \Delta T$, the expression simplifies to $\Delta \rho \approx -\rho_0 \gamma \Delta T$.

The percentage change in density is given by $\left| \dfrac{\Delta \rho}{\rho_0} \right| \times 100 = \gamma \Delta T \times 100$.

Given $\gamma = 49 \times 10^{-5} \text{ K}^{-1}$ and $\Delta T = 50^{\circ} \text{C} = 50 \text{ K}$.

Percentage change $= 49 \times 10^{-5} \times 50 \times 100 = 49 \times 50 \times 10^{-3} = 2450 \times 10^{-3} = 2.45$.

Answer: 2.45

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A cylinder of fixed capacity 44.81 contains hydrogen gas at STP. What is the amount of heat needed to raise the temperature of the gas in the cylinder by $20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ ? ($R=8.31 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}$)
questions.solution:
At STP, the volume of 1 mole of an ideal gas is $22.4 \text{ L}$.

Given the volume of the cylinder is $44.8 \text{ L}$, the number of moles $n$ of hydrogen gas is $n = \dfrac{44.8}{22.4} = 2 \text{ moles}$.

Hydrogen is a diatomic gas, so its molar heat capacity at constant volume $C_V$ is given by $C_V = \dfrac{f}{2}R$, where $f = 5$ is the degrees of freedom for a diatomic molecule.

$C_V = \dfrac{5}{2} \times 8.31 \text{ J mol}^{-1} \text{ K}^{-1} = 20.775 \text{ J mol}^{-1} \text{ K}^{-1}$.

The heat required $Q$ to raise the temperature by $\Delta T = 20^{\circ} \text{C}$ (which is equivalent to $20 \text{ K}$) at constant volume is $Q = n C_V \Delta T$.

$Q = 2 \times 20.775 \times 20 = 40 \times 20.775 = 831 \text{ J}$.

Answer: 831 J

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The latent heat of vaporisation of water is $2240 \mathrm{~J}$. If the work done in the process of vaporisation of $1 \mathrm{~g}$ is $168 \mathrm{~J}$, the increase in internal energy is
questions.solution:
According to the first law of thermodynamics, the heat supplied $Q$ is equal to the sum of the change in internal energy $\Delta U$ and the work done $W$ by the system during the process of vaporisation.

$Q = \Delta U + W$

Given that the latent heat of vaporisation $L = 2240 \text{ J}$ for $1 \text{ g}$ of water, the heat supplied $Q$ is $2240 \text{ J}$.

The work done $W$ during the process is given as $168 \text{ J}$.

Substituting these values into the equation:

$2240 \text{ J} = \Delta U + 168 \text{ J}$

Solving for the change in internal energy $\Delta U$:

$\Delta U = 2240 \text{ J} - 168 \text{ J}$

$\Delta U = 2072 \text{ J}$

Answer: 2072 J

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The dimension $[\mathrm{ML}^{-1} \mathrm{~T}^{-2}]$ is the physical quantity of
questions.solution:
The given dimension is $[M L^{-1} T^{-2}]$.

Pressure is defined as $\dfrac{\text{Force}}{\text{Area}} = \dfrac{[M L T^{-2}]}{[L^2]} = [M L^{-1} T^{-2}]$.

Energy density is defined as $\dfrac{\text{Energy}}{\text{Volume}} = \dfrac{[M L^2 T^{-2}]}{[L^3]} = [M L^{-1} T^{-2}]$.

Since both Pressure and Energy density have the dimension $[M L^{-1} T^{-2}]$, we evaluate the options provided.

Option (1) Energy density has the dimension $[M L^{-1} T^{-2}]$.

Option (2) Pressure \times Area is Force, which has dimension $[M L T^{-2}]$.

Option (3) Power \times Time is Energy, which has dimension $[M L^2 T^{-2}]$.

Option (4) $\dfrac{\text{Force}}{\text{Pressure}}$ is Area, which has dimension $[L^2]$.

Therefore, Energy density is the correct physical quantity.

Answer: Energy density

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Joule second is the unit of
questions.solution:
The unit of energy is Joule (J) and the unit of time is second (s).

The unit Joule second (J s) corresponds to the product of energy and time.

From the relation $E = h \nu$, where $E$ is energy and $\nu$ is frequency, the unit of Planck constant $h$ is $\dfrac{J}{s^{-1}} = J s$.

Angular momentum $L$ is defined as $L = mvr$. The dimensional formula for angular momentum is $[M L^2 T^{-1}]$.

The dimensional formula for energy is $[M L^2 T^{-2}]$. Multiplying by time $T$, we get $[M L^2 T^{-2}] \times [T] = [M L^2 T^{-1}]$.

Since the dimensions of energy multiplied by time are equivalent to the dimensions of angular momentum, the unit Joule second represents angular momentum.

Answer: Angular momentum

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A monochromatic light of wavelength $800 \mathrm{~nm}$ is incident normally on a single slit of width $0.020 \mathrm{~mm}$ to produce a diffraction pattern on a screen placed $1 \mathrm{~m}$ away. Estimate the number of fringes obtained in Young's double slit experiment with slit separation $0.20 \mathrm{~mm}$, which can be accommodated within the range of total angular spread of the central maximum due to single slit.
questions.solution:
The angular width of the central maximum in a single slit diffraction pattern is given by $\theta = \dfrac{2\lambda}{a}$, where $\lambda = 800 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m}$ and $a = 0.020 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$.

Substituting the values, $\theta = \dfrac{2 \times 800 \times 10^{-9}}{0.020 \times 10^{-3}} = \dfrac{1600 \times 10^{-9}}{20 \times 10^{-6}} = 80 \times 10^{-3} = 0.08 \text{ radians}$.

In Young's double slit experiment, the angular fringe width is $\beta_{\theta} = \dfrac{\lambda}{d}$, where $d = 0.20 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$.

Substituting the values, $\beta_{\theta} = \dfrac{800 \times 10^{-9}}{0.20 \times 10^{-3}} = \dfrac{800 \times 10^{-9}}{200 \times 10^{-6}} = 4 \times 10^{-3} = 0.004 \text{ radians}$.

The number of fringes $N$ that can be accommodated within the central maximum is the ratio of the total angular spread of the central maximum to the angular fringe width of the double slit experiment.

$N = \dfrac{\theta}{\beta_{\theta}} = \dfrac{0.08}{0.004} = 20$.

Answer: 20

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In Young's double slit experiment light of wavelength $500 \mathrm{~nm}$ is used to form interference pattern. A uniform glass plate of refractive index 1.5 and thickness $0.1 \mathrm{~mm}$ is introduced in the path of one of the interfering beams. The number of fringes that will shift due to this is
questions.solution:
The shift in the interference pattern in Young's double slit experiment when a glass plate of thickness $t$ and refractive index $\mu$ is introduced in the path of one of the beams is given by the formula:

$\Delta x = \dfrac{(\mu - 1)tD}{d}$

The number of fringes shifted $N$ is given by the ratio of the shift $\Delta x$ to the fringe width $\beta = \dfrac{\lambda D}{d}$.

$N = \dfrac{\Delta x}{\beta} = \dfrac{(\mu - 1)tD/d}{\lambda D/d} = \dfrac{(\mu - 1)t}{\lambda}$

Given values are $\mu = 1.5$, $t = 0.1 \text{ mm} = 0.1 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m} = 10^{-4} \text{ m}$, and $\lambda = 500 \text{ nm} = 500 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m} = 5 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}$.

Substituting these values into the formula:

$N = \dfrac{(1.5 - 1) \times 10^{-4}}{5 \times 10^{-7}}$

$N = \dfrac{0.5 \times 10^{-4}}{5 \times 10^{-7}}$

$N = \dfrac{0.5}{5} \times 10^{3} = 0.1 \times 1000 = 100$

Answer: 100

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Incident light of wavelength $\lambda=800 \mathrm{~nm}$ produces a diffraction pattern on a screen $1.5 \mathrm{~m}$ away when it passes through a single slit of width $0.5 \mathrm{~mm}$. The distance between the first dark fringes on either side of the central bright fringe is
questions.solution:
The condition for the first dark fringe in a single slit diffraction pattern is given by $a \sin \theta = n \lambda$, where $a$ is the slit width, $\lambda$ is the wavelength, and $n = 1$ for the first dark fringe.

Since $\theta$ is very small, $\sin \theta \approx \tan \theta = \dfrac{y}{D}$, where $y$ is the distance of the fringe from the central maximum and $D$ is the distance to the screen.

Substituting the values: $a \left( \dfrac{y}{D} \right) = \lambda \Rightarrow y = \dfrac{\lambda D}{a}$.

Given $\lambda = 800 \text{ nm} = 800 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m}$, $D = 1.5 \text{ m}$, and $a = 0.5 \text{ mm} = 0.5 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$.

$y = \dfrac{800 \times 10^{-9} \times 1.5}{0.5 \times 10^{-3}} = \dfrac{1200 \times 10^{-9}}{0.5 \times 10^{-3}} = 2400 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m} = 2.4 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m} = 2.4 \text{ mm}$.

The distance between the first dark fringes on either side of the central bright fringe is $2y = 2 \times 2.4 \text{ mm} = 4.8 \text{ mm}$.

Answer: 4.8 mm

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Two narrow parallel slits illuminated by a coherent monochromatic light produces an interference pattern on a screen
placed at a distance $\mathrm{D}$ from the slits. The separation between the dark lines of the interference pattern can be increased by
options: decreasing the distance between the screen and the slits
using monochromatic light of higher frequency
using monochromatic light of a longer wavelength
increasing the distance between the slits
questions.solution:
The fringe width $\beta$ in a Young's double slit experiment is given by the formula $\beta = \dfrac{\lambda D}{d}$, where $\lambda$ is the wavelength of the monochromatic light, $D$ is the distance between the slits and the screen, and $d$ is the separation between the two slits.

The separation between the dark lines (fringe width) is directly proportional to the wavelength $\lambda$ and the distance $D$, and inversely proportional to the slit separation $d$.

To increase the fringe width $\beta$, one must either increase $\lambda$, increase $D$, or decrease $d$.

Since frequency $f$ is related to wavelength by $\lambda = \dfrac{c}{f}$, using light of a higher frequency corresponds to a shorter wavelength, which would decrease the fringe width. Increasing the distance between the slits $d$ would also decrease the fringe width. Decreasing the distance $D$ would decrease the fringe width. Therefore, using light of a longer wavelength is the correct method to increase the fringe width.

Answer: using monochromatic light of a longer wavelength

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The number of possible natural oscillations of air column in a pipe closed at one end of length $85 \mathrm{~cm}$ whose frequencies lie below $1250 \mathrm{~Hz}$ are (velocity of sound $=340 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$)
questions.solution:
For a pipe closed at one end, the frequencies of natural oscillations are given by the formula $f_n = \dfrac{(2n-1)v}{4L}$, where $n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$ is the harmonic number, $v$ is the velocity of sound, and $L$ is the length of the pipe.

Given $v = 340 \text{ m/s}$ and $L = 85 \text{ cm} = 0.85 \text{ m}$.

Substituting the values into the formula:

$f_n = \dfrac{(2n-1) \times 340}{4 \times 0.85} = \dfrac{(2n-1) \times 340}{3.4} = (2n-1) \times 100 \text{ Hz}$.

We require $f_n \lt 1250 \text{ Hz}$, so:

$(2n-1) \times 100 \lt 1250$

$2n-1 \lt 12.5$

$2n \lt 13.5$

$n \lt 6.75$.

Since $n$ must be a natural number, the possible values for $n$ are $1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6$.

The number of possible natural oscillations is 6.

Answer: 6

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A scooter moves with a speed of $7 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$, on a straight road and is stopped by applying the brakes. Before stopping, the scooter travels $10 \mathrm{~m}$. If the weight of the scooter is $\mathrm{W}$, then the total resistance to the motion of the scooter will be
questions.solution:
Given initial speed $u = 7 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$, final speed $v = 0$, and distance $s = 10 \mathrm{~m}$.

Using the equation of motion $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$, we have $0 = 7^2 + 2a(10)$.

$0 = 49 + 20a \Rightarrow a = -\dfrac{49}{20} \mathrm{~ms}^{-2}$.

The retarding force $F$ is given by Newton's second law $F = ma = \dfrac{W}{g} a$.

Substituting the values, $F = \dfrac{W}{9.8} \times \left( -\dfrac{49}{20} \right)$.

Since $9.8 = \dfrac{98}{10} = \dfrac{49}{5}$, we have $F = \dfrac{W}{49/5} \times \left( -\dfrac{49}{20} \right) = W \times \dfrac{5}{49} \times \left( -\dfrac{49}{20} \right) = -\dfrac{5}{20} W = -\dfrac{1}{4} W$.

The magnitude of the resistance force is $\dfrac{1}{4} W$.

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{4} W$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: When water falls from a height of $80 \mathrm{~m}$ at the rate of $20 \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ to operate a turbine the losses due to frictional force are $20 \%$ of input energy. How much power is generated by the turbine?
questions.solution:
The potential energy of the water falling per unit time is the input power, given by $P_{in} = \dfrac{mgh}{t} = \left(\dfrac{m}{t}\right)gh$.

Given $\dfrac{m}{t} = 20 \text{ kg s}^{-1}$, $g = 10 \text{ m s}^{-2}$, and $h = 80 \text{ m}$, we have $P_{in} = 20 \times 10 \times 80 = 16000 \text{ W} = 16 \text{ kW}$.

The losses due to frictional force are $20 \%$ of the input energy, so the efficiency of the turbine is $100 \% - 20 \% = 80 \%$.

The power generated by the turbine is $P_{out} = 80 \% \text{ of } P_{in} = 0.8 \times 16 \text{ kW} = 12.8 \text{ kW}$.

Answer: 12.8 KW
